strengths: Novel Teacher-Student Distillation: Distilling specialized capabilities from multiple synthetic reinforcement learning (RL) experts trained with privileged depth information into a single RGB-only VLA student policy is an elegant and effective approach to bypassing the sim-to-real gap and 3D visual geometry bottleneck.

Capability-Balanced Data Aggregation: The proposed dynamic balanced data aggregation strategy based on Weighted Travel Time (WTT) effectively resolves the uneven capability acquisition during online DAgger-style training, ensuring faster and more stable training convergence.

Thorough Evaluation & Hardware Deployment: The method is validated both in complex simulation scenarios against established baselines (NavDP, ViPlanner, iPlanner) and on a physical Unitree GO2 robot, demonstrating robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in challenging real-world environments.

360-Degree Perception: Extending the VLA model to process multi-view (4 horizontal cameras) surround inputs provides the necessary spatial awareness to handle narrow squeezing and dynamic obstacle avoidance, surpassing single-view baselines.
weaknesses: Deployment and Latency Overhead: The model relies on a 7B-parameter LLM (Qwen2-7B) run on a powerful offboard server (NVIDIA RTX 5090) to achieve an inference speed of 7 Hz. This offboard execution introduces critical dependency on wireless communication stability and latency. If the network experiences packet loss or lag, the safety of the continuous velocity control could be compromised. Discussion on safety fallbacks or latency impacts in dynamic environments is missing.

Necessity of a Large VLA Model: The navigation task is framed around reaching specific relative coordinate goals (formatted as a textual prompt like 'Go to the position of <x: 10.00, y: 0.00>'). Because the goals are purely coordinate-based rather than semantic/open-ended, the open-world reasoning capacity of a 7B LLM is largely underutilized. The paper would be strengthened by comparing MM-Nav against a smaller, non-LLM multi-view model (e.g., standard ViT + GRU/Transformer policy) trained on the same dataset to justify the large parameter count.

Sim-to-Real Camera Alignment: The paper mentions using four fisheye cameras on the real robot, which are undistorted into perspective views. Details on the exact field of view (FOV) of these undistorted images, how they align with the simulation's camera settings (height, pitch, FOV), and how sensitive the model is to minor camera calibration errors are not fully explored.

strengths: The 360-degree surround-view configuration effectively addresses the limited field-of-view (FOV) drawback of many existing visual navigation systems, which is crucial for safety-critical behaviors like squeezing and dynamic avoidance.

Distilling from multiple specialized reinforcement learning (RL) experts trained with privileged depth maps allows the model to learn complex geometric behaviors (reaching, squeezing, and avoiding) without requiring explicit depth prediction during real-world inference.

The capability-balanced data aggregation strategy using Weighted Travel Time (WTT) dynamically balances training ratios, effectively preventing the catastrophic forgetting or neglect of harder skills like squeezing during online training.

Strong hardware validation on a quadruped robot (Unitree Go2) demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-real capability in challenging environments such as thin obstacle avoidance, glass walls, and dynamic human intrusions.
weaknesses: The 7 Hz inference rate, while acceptable for visual navigation, requires an offboard server equipped with a high-end desktop GPU (RTX 5090). This offboard setup introduces communication latency and limits the deployment of the robot in environments with weak wireless networks or outdoors where a local server is unavailable.

The reliance on custom-designed synthetic simulation environments to train the individual RL experts means that expanding to new capabilities (e.g., stair climbing, terrain-aware walking) would require substantial engineering effort to design new reward functions and simulators.

The continuous velocity action space ($v_x, v_y, v_{yaw}$) assumes an omnidirectional base. The paper does not discuss how easy or difficult it would be to adapt the action head to non-holonomic robots (such as standard wheeled differential-drive robots).

strengths: The paper addresses a challenging problem in visual navigation by introducing a multi-view (360-degree surround) Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that predicts continuous velocity commands, which is more suited for agile robot control than discrete action models.

The proposed capability-balanced DAgger framework effectively handles the uneven performance across different navigation tasks (reaching, squeezing, avoiding) by dynamically adjusting the data aggregation ratio.

The model is successfully deployed on a physical quadruped robot (Unitree Go2) and demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in diverse and challenging environments, achieving 7 Hz control loop speed.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison: All comparative baselines in Table I (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) are limited to a single front-facing camera. The proposed method utilizes a four-camera setup providing a 360-degree field of view. Consequently, it is unclear whether the performance improvements are primarily due to the superior sensing hardware/FOV or the proposed VLA training methodology. A multi-camera version of the baselines or a standard multi-camera architecture (e.g., ResNet+MLP) trained with standard DAgger should be included to isolate the contribution of the model architecture.

High computational footprint and offboard dependency: The policy relies on a 7B Qwen2 model, requiring an offboard server equipped with an RTX 5090 to achieve a modest 7 Hz inference rate. This offboard dependency introduces communication latency and risks of signal loss, which are undesirable for real-time safety-critical navigation. The paper would benefit from comparing against a smaller, onboard-capable model (e.g., <1B parameters or a standard CNN/ViT policy).

Under-scaled Mixed-RL baseline: In Table II, the Mixed-RL expert performs poorly, which the authors attribute to capacity limits of the small MLP. However, modern RL architectures can easily be scaled up (e.g., using larger networks or Transformers) to handle multi-task settings. Comparing against an under-optimized or small MLP baseline makes the claim regarding the 'synergy of VLA' less convincing.

Lack of implementation clarity: The paper does not specify whether the entire 7B LLM and SigLIP visual encoder are fully fine-tuned, or if parameter-efficient tuning methods (like LoRA) were utilized. This is critical for assessing the reproducibility and training resource requirements of the method.

strengths: Multi-expert distillation & capability balancing: The proposed strategy of training specialized RL experts with privileged depth information and then distilling their skills into a unified student VLA model is highly effective. The use of Weighted Travel Time (WTT) to dynamically balance the training data ratio across capabilities represents a robust solution to policy distribution shift.

Comprehensive 360-degree spatial awareness: Extending the visual tokenization of the VLA to process four surround-view camera views concurrently is an essential design choice that enables successful navigation in tight spaces (squeezing) and complex dynamic environments (avoiding).

Effective sim-to-real gap mitigation: Co-training the navigation policy with real-world Visual Question Answering (VQA) data aligns synthetic and real latent spaces effectively. This is well-demonstrated through quantitative real-world results and compelling UMAP latent visualizations.

Strong empirical performance: The model achieves state-of-the-art results on the InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark, outperforming existing baselines by a significant margin (88.1% success rate vs. 72.2% or 81.2% for the best baselines).
Real-world validation: The authors successfully deploy the 7B policy on a physical quadruped platform (Unitree Go2) in challenging indoor and outdoor scenarios with zero-shot transfer.
weaknesses: Hardware and edge deployment limitations: Running a 7B parameter VLA at 7 Hz requires offloading the inference to an external workstation equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. This reliance on offboard computation restricts deployment in regions with poor or unstable wireless connectivity.

High computational cost: Fine-tuning a 7B LLM on 8 H100 GPUs for several hours, followed by iterative online refinement phases, requires a massive compute budget that limits accessibility and democratization.

Complexity of RL expert training: The three separate reinforcement learning environments and reward functions (containing several task-specific hyperparameters) are complex. Reproducing these exact expert behaviors without a fully open-sourced simulator setup could prove challenging.

strengths: A well-designed and comprehensive visual navigation framework (MM-Nav) that elegantly combines 360-degree multi-view inputs, privileged RL expert distillation, and large-scale VQA co-training to bridge the sim-to-real gap.

The proposed capability-balanced online iterative training strategy (based on DAgger and weighted travel time) successfully addresses the problem of uneven skill performance across reaching, squeezing, and avoiding.

Impressive physical deployment and real-world experiments on a Unitree GO2 robot, demonstrating robust zero-shot sim-to-real performance in highly challenging scenarios (such as thin wire avoidance, narrow corridors, and nighttime navigation).

Substantial performance gains on established benchmarks: MM-Nav achieves an 88.1% success rate on the InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark, outperforming existing state-of-the-art baselines by a large margin (+15.9%).
Thorough ablation studies and visual analyses, such as the UMAP visualization showing how co-training on real-world VQA data aligns the representation spaces of synthetic and real observations.
weaknesses: Reliance on Offboard Computation: The policy is executed on a high-end remote server with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU rather than onboard. For real-world deployment, this introduces potential concerns regarding network latency, packet loss, or disconnection, which are not thoroughly discussed.

Clarification on Action Tokenization: The interface between the LLM (Qwen2) and the action head (MLP) is slightly unclear. It is mentioned that Qwen2 predicts an 'action token E_action' which is then mapped to continuous velocities via an MLP. It would be helpful to clarify if this is a newly introduced special token and whether predicting a single token is sufficient to represent multi-dimensional continuous velocity commands.

Lack of Geometry-Aware Auxiliary Supervision: Since the RL teachers use privileged depth maps while the student VLA uses RGB, the student must implicitly learn environmental geometry from actions alone. The paper could discuss whether adding an auxiliary depth estimation or feature distillation loss from the teacher's ResNet-18 features would further boost performance.

strengths: Pragmatic and Solid Pipeline: Distilling specialized RL experts (each trained under privileged depth information in customized scenarios) into a single 7B VLA model is a highly sensible and effective way to handle multiple navigation sub-tasks (reaching, squeezing, avoiding).

Dynamic Skill-Balancing: The proposed capability-balanced data aggregation (using Weighted Travel Time) is a well-designed modification of standard DAgger that prevents the model from neglecting complex tasks like squeezing or dynamic obstacle avoidance.

Strong Quantitative Results: The model shows excellent performance, achieving an 88.1% success rate on the public InternVLA-N1 benchmark, outperforming existing baselines by a significant margin (+15.9 points).

Physical Robot Validation: The zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is extensively validated on a Unitree GO2 quadruped robot in highly challenging scenarios (including thin wires, cluttered corridors, and transparent glass walls), which is a strong testament to the generalization capabilities of the model.

Insightful Visual and Latent Analysis: The analysis of VQA co-training using UMAP projections to show alignment of the latent distributions between simulator and real-world features is highly illustrative and convincing.
weaknesses: Inference Rate Constraints: Although 7 Hz is functional for slow quadruped locomotion, it is a borderline control rate for highly dynamic, agile navigation (e.g., fast running or drone flight). The computational load of a 7B parameter LLM limits the reactivity of the agent.

High Computational Overhead: Training requires significant resources (8 H100 GPUs for the initial VLA and iterative updates), making it difficult for research groups with limited resources to reproduce or build on top of this work.

Spatial Alignment in Tokenization: The multi-view visual tokenization concatenates tokens from front, right, back, and left views into a 1D sequence before feeding them into Qwen2. It is not fully clear if the transformer's self-attention can robustly model complex 3D spatial geometry out-of-the-box without explicit spatial embeddings or geometry-aware fusion layers.

Dependence on Sim-to-Real Fidelity of RL Teachers: Since the teachers rely entirely on depth maps, any significant discrepancy between the simulated depth maps (which are noise-free in IsaacLab) and real-world inputs could limit the expert actions' quality, although this is partially compensated by the VQA co-training.
